nameStory: The skilletfish gets its memorable name from its remarkably flattened body shape that resembles a cast-iron skillet when viewed from above. This pancake-flat profile is perfectly designed for its lifestyle of clinging to rocks and hiding in tight crevices along the rocky coast.
description: The skilletfish is a small, unusually flattened marine fish that rarely exceeds 4 inches in length. Its most distinctive feature is the powerful suction disk on its belly that allows it to cling tightly to rocks in turbulent coastal waters. The body is broad and flat like a pancake, with a large head that tapers to a narrow tail, giving it that characteristic skillet shape that earned it its common name.

idTips.label: Suction Disk
idTips.description: Large, circular suction disk on the belly feels rubbery to the touch and can grip surfaces with remarkable strength - you'll be amazed at how firmly these little fish can attach to rocks

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely flattened and broad, like a pancake or skillet, with the widest part at the head tapering dramatically toward the tail

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small fish typically 2-4 inches long, easily fitting in the palm of your hand

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Mottled brown and gray coloration that blends perfectly with rocky surfaces, often with darker blotches and lighter spots

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Dorsal and anal fins are positioned far back near the tail, with rounded pectoral fins that don't extend much beyond the body

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found clinging to rocks or hiding under stones in shallow coastal waters, especially in tide pools and rocky intertidal zones

habitat: Skilletfish inhabit rocky intertidal zones and shallow coastal waters throughout New England's coastline. You'll find them clinging to the undersides of rocks in tide pools, wedged into crevices between boulders, or attached to pier pilings and jetties. They prefer areas with strong wave action where their powerful suction disk gives them a survival advantage.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters begin to warm, often found in shallow tide pools during low tide where they're easier to spot against the rocks.
seasonality.summer: Peak observation season when they're most active and visible in tide pools and shallow rocky areas during warm, calm days.
seasonality.fall: Still readily found in tide pools but may move to slightly deeper water as temperatures cool, remaining attached to rocks and structures.
seasonality.winter: Less commonly observed as they move to deeper waters or remain hidden under rocks, though hardy individuals can still be found in protected tide pools.

funFact: A skilletfish's suction disk is so powerful that researchers have measured grip strengths over 150 times the fish's own body weight - imagine a human being able to hang from a ceiling while supporting the weight of a small car!
confusionNotes: Skilletfish are sometimes confused with small flounders or other flatfish, but remember that skilletfish are flattened from top to bottom (like being pressed by a book) while flounders are flattened side to side (like being squeezed in a vise). The telltale suction disk on the belly is the dead giveaway - no other New England fish has this feature.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'fish,' skilletfish belong to the clingfish family and are quite different from typical fish most people know. They're part of an ancient group that evolved specifically for life in the turbulent intertidal zone, making them living examples of extreme adaptation to harsh coastal environments.
compareHints: The skilletfish is the only clingfish species commonly found in New England waters, making it unique in our region. While other small coastal fish might share its rocky habitat preferences, no other species has the distinctive flattened body combined with a ventral suction disk. Its closest relatives are found in warmer tropical waters and have similar body plans but different color patterns and size ranges.
